Indonesia's palm oil exports are projected to fall 12% in 2027.
Our full range: https://lnkd.in/e338QDVJ

For buyers of palm derivatives, that is a supply-planning signal, not just a headline.

The projection sits alongside the country's B50 biodiesel mandate, which keeps more domestic palm oil at home. Reports also note that this policy shift may raise costs for India's edible oil industry in 2027. Add the EU traceability rules already reshaping export flows, and the direction is clear: less exportable volume, tighter compliance, more competition for certified material.

What this means practically for procurement teams:
1. Contract earlier. Forward coverage on key oleochemical and wax inputs could smooth 2027 exposure.
2. Lock specifications and origin now. Traceability documentation is becoming part of the buying decision, not an afterthought.
3. Diversify supply relationships before the squeeze, not during it.

Nothing here is a price forecast. Export policy, mandate timing and monsoon demand will all shape the outcome, and prices may move either way. But buyers who plan sourcing strategy ahead of a structural export shift tend to have more options than those who react.

WHY DID THE US PUT THESE FIVE COUNTRIES ON ITS AI CHIP WATCHLIST? 🇺🇸
🇸🇬 Singapore
🇲🇾 Malaysia
🇹🇭 Thailand
🇮🇩 Indonesia
🇧🇷 Brazil
Five countries, five different economies, and now one common concern from Washington: Who is actually getting access to advanced American AI chips?
On 16 November 2026, the US Commerce Department announced tighter export controls on advanced AI semiconductors, including additional licensing requirements for these five countries.
And no, this doesn't mean all five countries are banned from buying NVIDIA chips.
The rules are a little more complicated than that. 😂
FIRST, WHAT EXACTLY IS THE US RESTRICTING?
There are three important numbers and conditions:
1. 12 MILLION TPP
Data centres providing more than 12 million aggregate Total Processing Performance (TPP) to companies headquartered in restricted jurisdictions, including China, may trigger additional licensing requirements.
Even computing capacity across linked data centres can be counted together.
Importantly, this is a remote-computing threshold, NOT a blanket exemption for chip shipments below 12 million TPP to the five named countries.
2. 90 DAYS
Certain existing remote-computing arrangements will have 90 days from the effective date to obtain the required licence if they wish to continue operating.
3. US-HEADQUARTERED EXCEPTION
Certain shipments to US-headquartered companies, or companies with US-headquartered ultimate parents, are excluded from the new five-country licensing requirement, provided the required reporting conditions are met.
So the rules don't necessarily affect every operator equally.
BUT WHY THESE FIVE COUNTRIES?
Here's where their different roles in the AI industry matter.
🇸🇬 SINGAPORE — THE REGIONAL TECHNOLOGY & TRADING HUB
Singapore is a major centre for cloud services, semiconductor trading and regional technology operations.
Its role in cross-border technology supply chains makes chip movements and end-user verification particularly relevant.
The challenge? Maintaining its reputation as a trusted technology hub while navigating tighter US export controls.
🇲🇾 MALAYSIA — THE FAST-GROWING DATA CENTRE DESTINATION
Malaysia has attracted substantial data centre investment commitments, particularly around Johor.
The country is positioning itself as a regional destination for cloud and AI infrastructure.
But attracting investment is one thing. Ensuring operators can access advanced chips and serve compliant customers is another.
🇹🇭 THAILAND — THE EMERGING DATA CENTRE COMPETITOR
Thailand has been actively attracting cloud and data centre investments from international technology companies.
With different investors, operators and customer structures, additional licensing requirements could affect projects differently.
The question is whether regulatory procedures will influence future investment decisions and deployment timelines.
🇮🇩 INDONESIA — THE DOMESTIC DIGITAL ECONOMY
Indonesia has a large domestic market supporting demand for cloud computing, digital services and AI infrastructure.
Unlike facilities designed primarily to serve overseas computing customers, some Indonesian data centres focus on domestic demand.
That distinction could matter when assessing exposure to remote-computing restrictions.
🇧🇷 BRAZIL — LATIN AMERICA'S AI INFRASTRUCTURE AMBITION
Brazil is working to attract data centre investments through its energy advantages and investment incentives.
But cheaper infrastructure and favourable tax policies don't automatically guarantee access to the most advanced AI chips.
US export licensing could become another consideration for developers assessing new projects.
SO WHY DID WASHINGTON GROUP THEM TOGETHER?
According to the US Commerce Department, these five countries present a higher-than-normal risk of advanced semiconductor diversion.
The concern is that companies in restricted jurisdictions could access American computing technology through third countries.
Think about it.
A Chinese company might not be able to import certain advanced NVIDIA chips directly.
But what if it rents computing power from a data centre located overseas?
The chips never enter China.
The computing power can still be accessed remotely.
That's precisely the type of arrangement Washington is trying to control.
MY VIEW
I wouldn't interpret this as the end of AI infrastructure growth in these five countries.
But I do think it reveals something about the future of the AI industry.
Singapore is strengthening its position as a technology hub.
Malaysia is attracting data centre investments.
Thailand is competing for international infrastructure projects.
Indonesia is building capacity for its domestic digital economy.
Brazil wants to become a stronger AI infrastructure destination in Latin America.
Five different ambitions.
Yet access to some of the most advanced computing technology remains heavily influenced by US export policy.
And the implications won't necessarily be equal.
A US-linked hyperscaler, an independent GPU cloud provider and a data centre construction company can face very different commercial and regulatory exposures.
Having the land, electricity and billions in investment doesn't necessarily mean you control access to the technology.
Everyone wants a piece of the AI boom.
Apparently, Washington would also like to check the guest list. 😂
One final detail: The rule is scheduled for publication in the Federal Register on 19 November 2026 and is not yet effective as of 17 November.
Sources: US Department of Commerce / Bureau of Industry and Security (16 November 2026), Federal Register public inspection copy, Reuters.
For general information and market commentary only. Not investment advice.

According to reports from the Associated Press, PBS, and Al Jazeera, the Trump administration has issued new export control rules aimed at preventing Chinese companies from remotely accessing advanced U.S. computing chips and servers housed in third-party countries.

Key Details of the Rule
 * Targeted Countries: Announced by the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), the regulation introduces case-by-case export licensing requirements for advanced chip sales to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Brazil. The rule states that these nations present a "higher-than-normal risk of diversion" to unauthorized destinations.

 * Closing the Cloud Loophole: While existing U.S. export controls already ban the direct physical sale of top-tier AI hardware (such as Nvidia's most advanced chips) to China, Chinese developers have increasingly rented cloud computing power from overseas data centers, particularly in Southeast Asia to train and run AI models. The new rule requires overseas data centers serving clients in restricted countries (including China, Russia, Iran, and Cuba) to identify their end users and obtain U.S. licenses within 90 days.

 * Exemptions & Policy Shifts: According to TechCrunch, the rule exempts standard commercial recommendation systems used in e-commerce or social media. It also formally rescinds the Biden administration's January 2025 "AI Diffusion Rule," which the Trump administration argued placed unnecessary restrictions on U.S. companies and allies.

Context and Timing
News outlets note several converging factors behind the rollout of these restrictions:

 * Smuggling and Espionage Scrutiny: The rule follows heightened scrutiny and controversy surrounding chip smuggling networks (including the Megaspeed affair involving data centers in Southeast Asia) and pressure from the Treasury Department and National Security Council on the Commerce Department to tighten enforcement.

 * Diplomatic Timing: The announcement comes just days before President Donald Trump is scheduled to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China, during the APEC summit.

For developers in Nigeria and other emerging markets, the right configuration can make a practical difference:
🔹 Faster deployment
Factory assembly allows much of the internal piping, wiring and equipment integration to be completed before shipment, while the local team prepares the site.
🔹 Less on-site installation work
Clearly defined equipment packages and connections can simplify installation and help control local labor costs.
🔹 Solutions matched to the available gas supply
Pipeline-fed CNG stations, trailer-supplied daughter stations and L-CNG stations offer different routes to serving local demand.
🔹 Room to grow
A suitable modular design can support phased investment and future expansion as vehicle numbers and fuel demand increase.
Our approach starts with your gas source, target customers, daily demand and site conditions. From there, we develop a customized equipment configuration and coordinate installation guidance, commissioning and operator training.

80 formal candidate interviews in the past 10 weeks. Some findings.

Since early September I have held 80 candidate interviews for 11 different clients across APAC and Europe, each one a proper 30 minute call. On top of that come many more informal, casual conversations that never make it into a calendar.

The numbers behind it:

11 clients, from semiconductor equipment to aviation ground handling, food processing, agribusiness and automotive fastening.

14 different role types: finance manager, regional sales manager, channel director, key account manager, country manager China, business developer, operations lead, quality engineer and more.

Roughly 7-8 formal interviews per client before a shortlist is worth sending.

Searches running in Malaysia, China, Thailand, Indonesia, the Netherlands, Belgium and France at the same time. We are truly Nomilk2day International!

What stands out for me:

The talent is rarely where the job ad is. Many of the strongest candidates were not actively looking. They said yes because someone called them with a specific, honest story.

Sales and finance roles in technical industries are often hard to fill. Candidates need to understand the product and the numbers.

Every search is unique, and that is our strength. Knowing the client’s story and needs, and connecting them to the right talent, is what makes the difference. 

A question for you, whether you hire in manufacturing, food, agri or tech:

How many candidates do you like to talk to before you make an offer?
Which role has been open the longest, and what is it costing you each month?
Is your next key hire already working for someone else who has not noticed yet?

If one of those questions made you pause, send me a message. I am happy to share what we see in the market right now, no strings attached.

On the upcoming draft of Indonesia’s Intellectual Property Law, I had the honor of assisting Prof. Fajar Sugianto of Universitas Pelita Harapan (UPH), who was invited to the Indonesian House of Representatives (DPR RI) to provide expert recommendations to its Legislative Body (BALEG), particularly on the proposed Reversion Right. The discussion addressed whether the reversion of rights to creators and performers after 25 years should apply to existing buyout agreements, taking into account the principles of non-retroactivity and freedom of contract, as well as the appropriate transitional provisions.

The discussion also explored the economic implications of reversion rights for investment in music labels, producers, publishers, and the valuation of music catalogues. Drawing on Richard Posner’s Economic Analysis of Law, a central consideration is how intellectual property protection can be balanced with economic efficiency, investment certainty, and incentives for innovation. This also raises questions concerning statutory minimums, licensing mechanisms, and the appropriate degree of regulatory flexibility.

Further discussions concerned the allocation of legal liability among content creators, AI developers, and digital platforms for copyright infringement and the use of copyrighted works in AI training datasets. Issues surrounding opt-out mechanisms, collective licensing, dataset transparency, and algorithmic compliance raise a fundamental question, How can legislation effectively ensure that AI algorithms comply with the law?

When we talk about hotel swimming pools in tropical countries, heating is probably not the first thing that comes to mind.
But what about cooling?
In destinations such as Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and the Maldives, outdoor temperatures can remain high for much of the year. Under strong sunlight, pool water absorbs heat throughout the day. In some situations, the water can become warmer than guests would find comfortable for swimming.
A swimming pool is not always more comfortable when the water is warmer.
1. Hot Weather Can Make Pool Water Too Warm
Strong solar radiation, high outdoor temperatures and continuous exposure can gradually increase pool water temperature.
This can be particularly noticeable in:
Rooftop swimming pools
Shallow leisure pools
Pools with long hours of direct sunlight
Hotel pools in warm, humid climates
For guests looking to cool down after spending time outdoors, excessively warm pool water may reduce the comfort of the experience.
2. Wellness Trends Are Creating New Cooling Needs
Hotel pools are no longer just places for swimming.
Wellness facilities, spa pools, cold plunge pools and contrast bathing experiences are becoming more visible in the hospitality industry.
Guests may look for different water temperatures within the same property — a comfortable swimming pool, a warm spa pool and a cooler plunge pool.
This creates demand for more flexible water temperature management.
3. Pool Cooling Is Different from Air Conditioning
Cooling a hotel pool is not the same as cooling a hotel room.
It requires a dedicated water-side system that can remove heat from circulating pool water and maintain the desired temperature.
A reversible swimming pool heat pump can provide both heating and cooling, depending on the model and operating conditions.
For hotel operators, this can offer more flexibility throughout the year.
4. Does Every Tropical Hotel Need Pool Cooling?
Not necessarily.
The actual requirement depends on pool design, sunlight exposure, water volume, guest preferences and local climate.
Before selecting equipment, hotel operators and pool contractors should evaluate the desired water temperature, cooling capacity and daily operating conditions.
For pool contractors, hotel developers and equipment distributors, is pool cooling becoming a more important requirement in your market?

For years, the key challenges facing data centre developers have been securing sufficient power and utilities, suitable sites and connectivity.

A new U.S. export control regime suggests there may now be a fourth consideration: 

who is permitted to access the computing power those facilities provide.

The U.S. has introduced new restrictions aimed at preventing China-headquartered companies from accessing advanced AI computing power through data centres located outside China, including in Southeast Asia.

While previous export controls focused on where advanced AI chips could be shipped, the new rules increasingly focus on who can access and use that computing power remotely.

This could have important implications for data centre operators, developers, cloud providers, AI infrastructure businesses and investors across Indonesia, Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand.

In particular, businesses should be considering:

✅ Enhanced customer due diligence and beneficial ownership screening
✅ Export control compliance frameworks for AI and GPU infrastructure
✅ Potential impacts on customer mix, revenue forecasts and demand assumptions
✅ Additional M&A, financing and project development diligence requirements
✅ Contractual protections addressing compliance and regulatory risk

For Indonesia, this development is another reminder that digital infrastructure is increasingly operating at the intersection of technology, geopolitics and national security.

As AI infrastructure becomes more strategically important, I expect export controls and AI-related regulatory diligence to become increasingly important workstreams in data centre acquisitions, financings, joint ventures and development projects across Southeast Asia.

I've attached a short note summarising the new rules and some of the practical issues that data centre operators, investors and developers should be considering.

If your organisation is acquiring, developing, investing in, financing or operating data centre infrastructure in Southeast Asia, I would be pleased to discuss how these developments may affect your business.

A LUXURY VILLA. A CRYPTO PROJECT. A PROMISE OF HIGH RETURNS. WHAT COULD POSSIBLY GO WRONG?

Bali has become a destination for property investors, entrepreneurs and people looking for alternative investment opportunities.

Now imagine a project combining all three:
A luxury villa development.
An attractive rental ROI.
And a cryptocurrency or token offering supposedly providing additional upside, easier ownership or access to future profits.

It sounds innovative.
But before investing, I would ask a very different set of questions.

1. What is the actual underlying asset?
Is there a completed villa? A legally documented lease? Land held by a properly established entity? Or are you buying a digital token whose rights are not what the marketing suggests?

2. What exactly does the token give you?
Does it represent shares in a company, contractual rights to income, a debt claim or simply a digital asset whose price can fluctuate?
These are not interchangeable.
Owning a token does not automatically mean owning the land or the villa.

3. Where does the promised return come from?
Is it generated by real rental income after operating expenses?
Or does the investment depend on rising token prices, new buyers or assumptions about future demand?
A blockchain does not turn an unprofitable property into a profitable one.

4. Who protects your money?
Who holds the funds? Who controls the underlying asset? What happens if the developer fails, the platform closes or the token cannot be sold?

5. Can the investment survive without the crypto story?
This is the question I consider essential.
If the villa cannot justify its acquisition price through realistic operating performance, why should adding a cryptocurrency make the investment more attractive?

Technology may change how investments are structured or transferred. It does not remove construction risk, leasehold risk, legal risk or the realities of hospitality operations.

Indonesia has been developing a regulatory framework for digital financial assets, including crypto assets, and the Financial Services Authority (OJK) has reported property-related tokenisation models passing its regulatory sandbox process. That is a reason to examine the actual legal structure carefully, not to assume every tokenised property offer is approved or protected.

My position is simple.
I am not against innovation.
I am against investors being asked to trust a sophisticated story before they understand the underlying business.

Before committing your money, independently verify the property, the legal rights, the operating figures, the token structure and the regulatory position.
First, understand the asset. Then understand the investment. Only then consider the technology.

Because the most modern investment structure in the world cannot compensate for a bad deal underneath it.

#Bali #Crypto #RealEstateInvestment #Blockchain #PropertyInvestment #DueDiligence

Geography alone no longer guarantees compute access.

AI’s next edge sits at the intersection of capacity, compliant access and efficient execution.

Ylang ylang is a classic floral raw material widely used in fragrance formulas, mainly cultivated in Southeast Asia. Its large, striking flower earns it the local title “Queen of Flowers”. It delivers a warm, sweet aroma, blending fruity hints and balsamic undertones, which brings soft, sensual charm to perfume compositions.
 
Its scent profile shares similarities with absolute jasmine, so it is sometimes nicknamed “poor man’s jasmine”. However, the price gap between different grades of ylang ylang essential oil is substantial, which is a key point for fragrance developers and buyers.
 
There is a long-circulated myth: ylang ylang works as an aphrodisiac.
 
This story originated from Indonesia, where ylang ylang blossoms were traditionally used to decorate wedding chambers. Locals believed its scent could bring harmony and happiness to couples. As the story spread, it was exaggerated and labelled as an aphrodisiac.
 
Scientific findings tell us a different truth. Studies show ylang ylang essential oil can help ease discomfort, lower blood pressure and calm the pulse. Instead of stirring excitement, it soothes nervousness and quiets restless emotions.
 
It is a versatile floral building block for oriental, chypre and romantic floral fragrances. Many of our OEM custom scents use graded ylang ylang to enrich the heart notes, adding rounded, sweet floral depth without being cloying.
 
Let’s stop over-mystifying ylang ylang. It is simply a beautiful, valuable floral ingredient.

🔊 WHAT IF THE NEXT GENERATION OF ACOUSTIC MATERIALS STARTED WITH A COCONUT HUSK? 🥥

When we think about acoustic panels, we often picture synthetic foam, mineral wool, fiberglass, or other conventional materials.
But what about natural fibers?

🌴 Coconut husk containscocofiber—a material traditionally associated with ropes, mats, brushes, and various industrial applications. Its potential may extend much further.

🔬 Natural fibers are an interesting area of acoustic material research because their fibrous structures can help dissipate sound energy under suitable material and design conditions.

This raises an interesting question:
COULD COCOFIBER BECOME A MATERIAL OPTION FOR ACOUSTIC-PANEL DEVELOPMENT?

For manufacturers and material developers exploring this possibility, several characteristics deserve attention:
🧵 1. FIBER STRUCTURE
Fiber length, distribution, thickness, and consistency can influence the structure and properties of the resulting acoustic material.
📐 2. DENSITY AND THICKNESS
These are important design variables that can influence the sound absorption characteristics of a fibrous panel.
🌬️ 3. POROSITY AND AIRFLOW RESISTANCE
The arrangement of fibers and the resulting pore structure influence how sound waves interact with and travel through the material.
🧱 4. MATERIAL COMPOSITION
Binders, backing materials, fiber treatment, and overall panel construction can influence the final acoustic and mechanical properties.
🔥 5. SAFETY AND DURABILITY
Fire performance, moisture resistance, dimensional stability, and long-term behavior must be evaluated for the intended application.

⚠️ ONE IMPORTANT DISTINCTION: SOUND ABSORPTION IS NOT THE SAME AS SOUNDPROOFING.
An acoustic panel may help reduce reflected sound and reverberation inside a room.
However, that does not automatically mean it can prevent sound from travelling between rooms.

The opportunity is not to claim that cocofiber can immediately replace conventional acoustic materials. It is to explore whether this agricultural fiber can be engineered into a material that meets specific acoustic, mechanical, safety, and commercial requirements.

📈 THIS IS WHERE MATERIAL INNOVATION BECOMES INTERESTING.
An agricultural by-product can become the starting point for research and development in an entirely different industrial sector.

💬 Could coconut fiber have a place in the future of acoustic materials?
We welcome perspectives from acoustic engineers, interior-material manufacturers, architects, and material developers.

Why Civil Engineers Should Understand Spatial Planning — Not Just Construction.
One of the most valuable perspectives in civil engineering is understanding what happens before a project reaches the construction stage.
A development project may be technically feasible but still face significant challenges due to land-use regulations, infrastructure limitations, or spatial planning requirements.
Before starting construction, several important questions should be addressed:
1. Land Use Compatibility
Is the proposed development consistent with the applicable spatial planning framework?
2. Infrastructure Accessibility
Can existing roads, drainage networks, and utilities support the proposed development?
3. Site Constraints
Are there flood risks, environmental limitations, elevation differences, or other physical constraints?
4. Regulatory Considerations
What spatial planning and development requirements apply to the project?
5. Long-Term Development Impact
How will the project interact with surrounding infrastructure and future urban growth?
These considerations are particularly relevant in rapidly developing urban areas.

In 2010 a small Jakarta team gave local developers something to be proud of. On 25 May 2010, Yahoo announced it had acquired Koprol, an Indonesian location-based social network. Koprol launched in February 2009 and worked straight from an ordinary phone browser, no GPS and no special app needed. You checked in to a place and saw who else was there.

Why it still matters to me: Koprol won because it was built for the phones Indonesians actually carried back then, not the phones we wished they had. But the story is also a warning. In mid 2012 Yahoo decided to shut the service down, and a month later it handed the trademark and domain rights back to the founders.

The lesson for me: learn your users' real devices and habits, and build from there. And don't assume that being bought by a big player means your product is safe forever. If you're building an app today, have you tried it on your users' most basic phone?

🚨 The U.S. restricted chip exports to China. Now it’s targeting who can rent the computing power.

A Chinese AI company can train a model on advanced GPUs without bringing a single chip into China. It can rent computing power from a data center abroad. A new U.S. Commerce Department rule targets that route.

Under the rule, overseas data centers already supplying significant computing power to China-based companies must obtain a U.S. license within 90 days of the rule taking effect to continue those services. The rule also imposes licensing requirements on certain advanced-chip exports to Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brazil.

For AI developers, access to GPUs can determine which models they can train and how quickly. And for Washington, enforcing chip controls now means looking beyond where the hardware ships to who uses it remotely.

Can Washington control access to computing power when the chips and their users are in different countries?

The US has issued a rule aimed at Chinese companies accessing advanced AI chips through overseas data centers.

Reuters reports that the rule also requires companies in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brazil to seek US export licenses for the most advanced chips. The Commerce Department says the goal is to prevent remote computing arrangements from circumventing existing restrictions.

For cloud operators, the practical question is how to check both the destination of hardware and the customers who can use it. More diligence could add time and cost to sales. For AI developers, the availability of rented compute may depend on where a provider operates and which customers it serves.

The rule could also complicate capacity planning. A data center can commit capital to chips and facilities years before it knows how licensing and enforcement will affect its customer base. The scale of those effects remains uncertain.

When evaluating an overseas AI infrastructure contract, how should buyers and providers divide responsibility for customer checks and licensing risk?

THE CALVO BRIEF - NOVEMBER 16, 2026

BLUF: The most important export-control development today is not a new sanctions designation or an ITAR amendment. It is a BIS pre-publication rule that could bring remote access to advanced computing firmly into the EAR compliance process.

On November 15, BIS released a draft interim final rule titled “Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors.” The rule is not yet operative. BIS says it will take effect upon Federal Register publication, but the posted version still contains blank publication, docket, and deadline fields. Companies should prepare now, but confirm the final text before making a legal determination.

The proposed new section 744.24 would require a license when a party knows that covered advanced-computing items will support a data center providing more than twelve million aggregate TPP, through one facility or linked facilities, to or for a company headquartered, or ultimately parented, in Macau or a Country Group D:5 destination. The principal items include ECCNs 3A090 and 4A090 and related dot-z hardware, software, and technology.

The draft also adds destination-based license requirements for covered items going to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil. A U.S.-headquartered consignee or end user may qualify for an exclusion but only with monthly reporting under proposed section 743.10. Existing foreign data centers serving Macau or D:5-headquartered companies would have 90 days from the effective date to obtain a license.

Here is an illustrative example. A U.S. company plans to export 4A090 servers to a Malaysian data center owned by a U.S. parent. The facility will rent compute to a Chinese model developer through several linked campuses. The physical destination triggers the proposed Malaysia rule. The U.S. parent exclusion would depend on reporting And if the linked capacity exceeds 12 million aggregate TPP, the remote Chinese customer may independently trigger section 744.24. The exporter should pause, identify the ultimate customer and parentage, calculate combined TPP, and determine whether a license or exclusion applies.

The immediate steps are to map foreign data center deployments and remote users, verify ultimate-parent ownership, and build contractual notice, monitoring, licensing, and reporting controls before the final rule becomes effective.

I’m Attorney Francisco Javier Calvo. Follow for daily OFAC, ITAR, EAR, and national security updates. 

This is general information, not legal advice.

The AI race won't be won by the smartest model alone. It will be won by whoever can turn intelligence into economic impact at scale.

There is an interesting debate happening in the industry about who is actually leading the AI frontier.

Is it model performance? Intelligence per dollar? Token consumption? Benchmark results?

All are relevant metrics. But I think we're missing a bigger question:

How effectively can we translate frontier AI into real-world economic value?

Looking at Indonesia, the opportunity is particularly interesting.

Consider a few data points:

🇮🇩 AI adoption is accelerating. The latest e-Conomy SEA 2026 report by Google, Temasek and Bain highlights that 54% of Indonesia's working population is already using generative AI.

🇮🇩 The economic opportunity is substantial. Research by Public First estimates that effective AI adoption by Indonesian organizations could contribute Rp620 trillion in economic value by 2030.

🇮🇩 Infrastructure matters. Google's Jakarta Cloud Region has already contributed an estimated Rp900 trillion to Indonesia's economy between 2020 and 2025, according to Public First research.

These numbers tell us something important.

The next phase of AI competition isn't simply about who builds the most intelligent model.

It's about who can bring together five critical capabilities:

1. Frontier intelligence: Building increasingly capable models and AI agents.
2. Infrastructure: Providing the compute, cloud and data foundations to scale.
3. Enterprise data: Connecting AI to trusted, governed and business-critical information.
4. Security and sovereignty: Making AI deployable in highly regulated industries.
5. Ecosystem: Enabling developers, partners and enterprises to innovate together.

This is where I believe Google has a compelling competitive position.

The combination of Gemini, Vertex AI, BigQuery, Google Distributed Cloud and its expanding infrastructure creates an integrated foundation for organizations to move from AI experimentation to enterprise-scale adoption.

And importantly, enterprises don't necessarily want to be locked into one model. They want the flexibility to choose the right intelligence for the right business problem.

For Indonesia, think about banking, telecommunications, manufacturing, healthcare and public services.

The real AI race is no longer just about winning the model race.

It's about building the intelligent economy.

Indonesia just put 38.6 million hectares on the jurisdictional REDD+ map. The paperwork is the easy part.
 
At COP31 on 11 November, Indonesia registered its TREES Concept document under ART, covering nine provinces and about 40% of its forest cover (ANTARA News, 12 Nov 2026).

But project developers now have to nest inside the provincial baseline, or the same tonne is counted twice. Indonesia’s own Deputy Forestry Minister flagged double counting as the thing to prevent.
 
Five of the nine provinces are filed as high forest, low deforestation. Anyone who has measured intact forest knows the hard part there is proving the threat, not counting the carbon.
 
For developers working in Asia, is nesting a way to share risk, or a quiet squeeze on margins?

Who is going to supply the electricity for the next 10 years?

Across Asia, governments are planning enormous expansions in electricity infrastructure.

Vietnam has set ambitious targets for its national power infrastructure.

Delivering reliable gigawatts is another.

Gas turbine manufacturers are facing years of delivery backlogs.

Transmission infrastructure requires substantial investment.

Grid connections, fuel supply, approvals and financing all take time.

And the demand is not coming from AI data centres alone.

Manufacturing, electric vehicles, semiconductor factories, industrial parks and ordinary households are all competing for electricity.

So here's the question.

Will countries have to wait until 2035 for their power infrastructure to catch up?

Or can a combination of smarter grid investment, dedicated power generation, renewable energy, storage and private-sector participation shorten the timeline?

For developers, one lesson is becoming increasingly clear.

The value of a project is no longer determined by how many MW it announces — but how many MW it can actually deliver, and when.

posts.text:
AI training and copyright: three courts, three answers

In ten days, courts in Europe, Canada and the US each moved on the same question: can an AI company train on copyrighted work without permission?

🇪🇺 European Union (3 November)
In Like Company v. Google (C-250/25), Advocate General Szpunar said training is "as a rule, freely permitted" under the text-and-data-mining exception, if developers:
• use only lawfully accessible sources
• respect machine-readable opt-outs such as robots.txt
• take steps to stop the model reproducing specific works
But a chatbot fetching and reusing news in real time may still infringe press publishers' rights.

🇨🇦 Canada (13 November)
The Ontario Court of Appeal unanimously held that OpenAI must defend the Canadian news publishers' suit in Ontario. OpenAI argued that its training happened outside the province. The Court found "a real and substantial connection". Canadian fair dealing, not US fair use, will apply, and there is no text-and-data-mining exception. This decides venue only.

🇺🇸 United States (pending)
In In re OpenAI Copyright Infringement Litigation, Judge Sidney Stein will decide fair use on cross-motions for summary judgment, without a trial. On 6 November he allowed 56 amicus briefs.

🇮🇳 And India?
In ANI v. OpenAI, the Delhi High Court (24 July) kept jurisdiction, held training-related storage prima facie covered by Section 52(1)(a)(i), and refused an interim injunction. ANI's appeal is pending. Indonesia is legislating instead, and Google, Meta and TikTok opposed its bill on 11 November.

Three patterns across the courts:
1️⃣ Location isn't a shield. Delhi and Ontario both rejected "we trained abroad".
2️⃣ Opt-outs matter. The EU makes them the line, and the Delhi HC weighed the unused crawler opt-out against ANI.
3️⃣ Outputs are the weak point. Regurgitation is where liability sits.

My take: India shouldn't leave this to one interim order. Stretching "private use, including research" to cover commercial AI training is a fragile base for a whole industry. A clear statutory rule with opt-outs, transparency and anti-memorisation duties would serve creators and developers better.

📎 Resources:
• CJEU press release: https://lnkd.in/dt_HFY-H
• CTV on Ontario: https://lnkd.in/d2tEwBtS
• IPWatchdog on the US briefs: https://lnkd.in/dyZ5zdRs
• LiveLaw on ANI: https://lnkd.in/dENAP_-c

Which approach should India take: fair dealing, an opt-out exception, or licensing?

Views are personal; for general information only. The AG opinion is non-binding and the other matters are pending.

Indonesia PPP Investment Watch | Regional Capacity Building

Tasikmalaya Identifies Street Lighting, Markets, and Hospitals as Potential PPP Sectors

The Government of Tasikmalaya Regency held a dissemination program on Public-Private Partnership / KPBU for infrastructure provision on 12 November 2026.

The program was attended by Tasikmalaya’s regional leadership and was intended to strengthen understanding of KPBU as an infrastructure-delivery and public-service improvement mechanism.

The regional government emphasized that KPBU should not be viewed only as a way to secure financing outside the regional budget.

It should also be used to:

• Improve infrastructure-delivery efficiency
• Strengthen public-service quality
• Allocate risks appropriately
• Support long-term infrastructure performance
• Encourage private-sector expertise and innovation

Regional government agencies were asked to begin identifying and mapping infrastructure needs in their respective sectors.

Priority should be given to projects that:

• Address urgent infrastructure needs
• Provide broad public benefits
• Have measurable service requirements
• May be suitable for private-sector participation
• Can potentially be developed through KPBU

Three sectors were specifically identified for further assessment:

• Public street lighting
• Public markets
• Hospitals and healthcare infrastructure

$$70.9 billion of Article 6 carbon credits could reach the market by
2030. Governments have signed contracts for $1.6 billion of it.

That is the main finding of the State of the Article 6 Carbon Market
2026, which the Article 6 Network launched at COP31 in Antalya on 13
November. The report counts about 2.36 billion tonnes of known supply
to 2030. Sovereign buyers have contracted about 53 million tonnes.
That is 2.2% of the supply.

New to this? Article 6 is the part of the Paris Agreement that lets
one country pay for emission cuts made in another and count them
toward its own climate target. The report prices every tonne at $30.
So $70.9 billion is what the supply would be worth if every known
tonne found a buyer at that price. Today, about 98 of every 100 tonnes
have no contract.

If you develop renewable, biochar or biogas projects in India and hope
to sell to a foreign government one day, keep this gap in mind before
you plan your revenue.

Why it matters
130 Parties now have an Article 6 authority, and governments have signed 113 bilateral agreements. Nine in ten tonnes of planned Article 6.2 outcomes have no named sovereign buyer yet. Only about 151,566 tonnes have actually moved between countries so far. New tenders and deals since October 2025 add 27.3 million tonnes, worth $819 million, including Singapore's tender and Norway's purchase of up to 12 million tonnes from Indonesia. Estimated demand from national climate targets to 2030 is about 200million tonnes, or $6 billion.

What was not disclosed
• Real contract prices. The $30 a tonne is the report's own
assumption, based on the Swiss KliK Foundation's average
• How much of the 2.36 billion tonnes will pass registration and
host-country authorisation
• A country-by-country split in the public summary

Our takeaway at GreenLoop
For project developers: in this market the buyer is the scarce part. Start buyer talks while you design the project, well before the first issuance.
For dMRV: Norway's government says it pays only for cuts that are carried out, verified and delivered. Data a buyer can check makes that last step shorter.
Tenders are where new sovereign demand shows up. The report names
Singapore, Norway, Germany, Switzerland and Taiwan as active buyers.

At GreenLoop we help Indian project developers get buyer-ready, with
digital MRV built in from day one.

If you were starting a project today, would you sign a buyer first, or
build the supply and find a buyer later?

Tabanan Redesigns Gadarata Market PPP to Improve Investor Attractiveness

The Government of Tabanan Regency has revised the planned design for the revitalization of Gadarata Main Market as part of its efforts to improve the project’s investment feasibility.

The proposed development is being prepared under Indonesia’s Public-Private Partnership / KPBU framework.

Under the revised design, all market buildings will be standardized at four storeys. Earlier plans included buildings with different heights, with some structures reaching six storeys.

The redesign is intended to:

• Reduce construction requirements
• Lower the project’s investment cost
• Improve commercial feasibility
• Increase private-sector interest
• Align the building design with applicable regional requirements

Project preparation status:

• Site area: approximately 1.6 hectares
• Scheme: PPP/KPBU
• Current stage: Project and tender-document preparation
• Project Development Facility support: Ministry of Finance
• Project-preparation assistance: PT Penjaminan Infrastruktur Indonesia / PT PII
• Indicative tender target: 2027

The final investment value following the redesign has not yet been confirmed.

The commercial-development concept is expected to remain part of the plan, including:

• Space for traditional market traders
• Cinema facilities
• A city hotel
• Supporting commercial activities

The regional government has stated that traditional traders will continue to receive space within the proposed development.

Why it matters:

Traditional-market revitalization requires a balance between public-service responsibilities and commercial viability.

Reducing the project’s capital requirement may improve investor appetite, but commercial attractiveness must still be balanced with:

• Trader affordability
• Appropriate relocation arrangements
• Market accessibility
• Public-service standards
• Long-term operations and maintenance
• Revenue-generation assumptions
• Fiscal affordability
• Transparent procurement

Investor takeaway:

Gadarata Market represents an emerging example of urban-market revitalization through KPBU.

The redesign may make the project more attractive to prospective investors, but participation will only be confirmed through the formal procurement process.

Market operators, property developers, hospitality companies, infrastructure investors, lenders, and transaction advisors should monitor completion of the project documents and the official tender announcement targeted for 2027.

CwAI:

# 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗔𝗜 𝗪𝗔𝗥 𝗠𝗔𝗬 𝗡𝗢𝗧 𝗕𝗘 𝗪𝗢𝗡 𝗕𝗬 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗕𝗜𝗚𝗚𝗘𝗦𝗧 𝗚𝗣𝗨. 𝗜𝗧 𝗠𝗔𝗬 𝗕𝗘 𝗪𝗢𝗡 𝗕𝗬 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗕𝗘𝗦𝗧 𝗔𝗣𝗣𝗟𝗜𝗖𝗔𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡.

Was the Jensen Huang–NVIDIA crisis a Chinese pre-emptive strike on America's AI industry?

It is a provocative thesis, not an established fact. US reporting describes an investigation into Alice Huang's alleged links to Chinese intelligence; the allegations remain unproven and Beijing denies them. Jensen Huang acknowledged an affair and Reuters reported his resignation as NVIDIA CEO on November 12. But no public evidence proves Beijing orchestrated the affair or engineered a US AI financing crisis.

Still, the strategic vulnerability deserves attention.

NVIDIA became more than a chip supplier. It sits at the intersection of GPUs, AI-cloud customers, strategic investments and data-centre finance. GPUs can support asset-backed lending; NVIDIA investments can help customers expand capacity—and buy more NVIDIA hardware.

That is not automatically fraud. The risk is concentration: if confidence, collateral values and customer funding weaken together, the network can transmit the shock.

But the bigger shift may matter more than the scandal.

AI is moving from one-size-fits-all closed models towards specialised services. Think of the Windows era: a common platform enabled thousands of applications for accounting, banking, insurance and manufacturing. Open-weight models could do the same for AI.

Developers need not train frontier models. They can adapt existing models, connect company data and build applications for claims, credit, tax, reconciliation, fraud detection and investment research.

𝗡𝗼𝘁 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆 𝘁𝗮𝘀𝗸 𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗱𝘀 𝗮𝗻 𝗡𝗩𝗜𝗗𝗜𝗔 𝗚𝗣𝗨.

Frontier training and heavy inference still need powerful accelerators. But document processing, rules engines, orchestration and smaller-model inference can often run economically on CPUs. The future is heterogeneous computing—not GPU-or-nothing.

Palantir illustrates the application layer: connecting models to enterprise data and real workflows. It has not replaced NVIDIA with its own chips; its AI partnerships also include NVIDIA. Application software may capture enormous value.

The economic disruption:

• Intelligence becomes cheaper.  
• Industry expertise becomes more valuable.  
• Smaller firms can build specialized AI products.  
• Productivity spreads beyond hyperscalers.  
• Hardware choices become more diverse.

China's open-weight ecosystem could benefit—but so can developers everywhere, including Indonesia.

The contest may not be whose model is smartest. It may be who embeds useful, affordable AI into millions of organizations.

NVIDIA helped build the engine room of the AI boom. The next wave may belong to application builders.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗚𝗣𝗨 𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝘂𝗻𝘄𝗮𝘆. 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗹𝗶𝗰𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗼𝗺𝘆 𝗺𝗮𝘆 𝘁𝗮𝗸𝗲 𝗼𝗳𝗳 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗶𝘁.

🚨 AI won't replace recruiters.
But recruiters who use AI well will close hires 2x faster than those who don't.
Last month, my AI-assisted workflow helped me shortlist 6 AI engineers in Singapore in 4 days — for a role that had been open for 2 months.
Here's how I use AI + my ATS across the FULL hiring cycle 👇

1⃣ INTAKE ChatGPT/Claude turns a vague JD into a clear checklist: must-haves vs. nice-to-haves + smart questions for the hiring manager call.

2⃣ MARKET INTEL Perplexity Pro shows which companies are hiring a skill in SG/MY — with source links, so I verify everything myself.

3⃣ SOURCING AI drafts Boolean strings & similar titles (SRE, Platform Engineer, MLOps...). Then I hunt where candidates actually are: LinkedIn Recruiter, GitHub, JobStreet, Naukri, Indeed. → AI drafts. I decide.

4⃣ SCREENING — MY SKILL MATRIX 📊 A report card for every resume: ✅ proof shown • 🟡 needs checking • ❌ ask directly.

For an AI Engineer role: ✅ LLM fine-tuning — resume shows a project with real accuracy results → strong proof 🟡 RAG pipelines — mentioned, no outcomes → probe in screening ❌ MLOps — not shown → ask in the call

How the tools fit in, every day: 🤖 ChatGPT & Claude → build the checklist + draft screening questions 🤖 Gemini → explains any new tech in plain English in minutes 🧑‍💼 Me → I read every resume and make the final call. AI prepares. I decide.
I strip personal details first — fair hiring, every time.

5⃣ OUTREACH AI writes draft #1. I rewrite it around the candidate's real story. Copy-paste messages get ignored.

6⃣ OFFER, COMPLIANCE & JOINING Salary negotiation — where the human conversation matters most. For Singapore: EP rules, CPF, TAFEP fair-hiring checks, BGV. I verify every rule myself.

7⃣ ATS = SINGLE SOURCE OF TRUTH Workday • Ceipal • Zoho • Bullhorn — every stage tracked. No candidate falls through the cracks.
That's how I keep an ~80% offer-to-join ratio. 📈

⚠️ MY 3 NON-NEGOTIABLE RULES: 🔒 No confidential data in public AI tools ✅ Verify facts & regulations before sharing 🧠 AI never makes the hiring decision. People do.
Tools are the easy part. Trust, speed and market knowledge close the offer. 🤝

posts.text:
80 formal candidate interviews in the past 10 weeks. Some findings.

Since early September I have held 80 candidate interviews for 11 different clients across APAC and Europe, each one a proper 30 minute call. On top of that come many more informal, casual conversations that never make it into a calendar.

The numbers behind it:

11 clients, from semiconductor equipment to aviation ground handling, food processing, agribusiness and automotive fastening.

14 different role types: finance manager, regional sales manager, channel director, key account manager, country manager China, business developer, operations lead, quality engineer and more.

Roughly 7-8 formal interviews per client before a shortlist is worth sending.

Searches running in Malaysia, China, Thailand, Indonesia, the Netherlands, Belgium and France at the same time. We are truly Nomilk2day International!

What stands out for me:

The talent is rarely where the job ad is. Many of the strongest candidates were not actively looking. They said yes because someone called them with a specific, honest story.

Sales and finance roles in technical industries are often hard to fill. Candidates need to understand the product and the numbers.

Every search is unique, and that is our strength. Knowing the client’s story and needs, and connecting them to the right talent, is what makes the difference. 

A question for you, whether you hire in manufacturing, food, agri or tech:

How many candidates do you like to talk to before you make an offer?
Which role has been open the longest, and what is it costing you each month?
Is your next key hire already working for someone else who has not noticed yet?

If one of those questions made you pause, send me a message. I am happy to share what we see in the market right now, no strings attached.

This visit is part of a long-standing annual tradition between our offices. Each year, representatives from Indonesia visit our HQ in Japan, and our Japanese colleagues travel to Bandung, to exchange knowledge, share best practices, and strengthen the bond between our teams.

This year, our discussions centred on a challenge that is reshaping the way engineers work in Japan. Under the Work Style Reform legislation, overtime is now capped at 45 hours per month and 360 hours per year, and since April 2024 these limits have also applied to the construction sector. The working hours have become shorter, but the workload has not. So the key question is: "how do they stay fully compliant while remaining effective and efficient?"

Our colleagues shared how they work alongside existing software and AI tools, and how they keep refining their prompts until they find workflows that are faster and more practical, while still keeping every result verified and accurate.

At Fujicon Priangan Perdana, we are on the same journey. We keep exploring how AI can help us work more carefully, more precisely, and more efficiently.
One of the most memorable moments came during the Q&A session, when part of Fujicon Priangan Perdana, Mas RIO DJANERI asked the question (and maybe many of us have quietly wondered about?!): “Is AI a threat to us as modellers and engineers? Will our jobs eventually be replaced?”

The President of Fuji Planning Consultant and the CEO of Fujicon Priangan Perdana, PakAndhitiawarman Nugraha answeredthat has been echoing in my mind ever since:
"An engineer will not be replaced by AI, but by an engineer who works smartly with AI.
Likewise, A Modeller will not be replaced by AI, but by a Modeller who works smartly with AI.
AI has no purpose of its own unless someone drives it. A good prompt can only come from someone who understands the context, the background, and the engineering fundamentals behind the problem. Expertise is still the foundation."

AI is here to stay, and it is not something we can simply stop. But we can choose how we respond to it. Used wisely and appropriately, AI is not a threat. It is a partner that helps us do our work better.

So, AI: friend or threat? The answer depends on how well we learn to use it. 😊 

My sincere thanks to the Fuji Planning Consultant team for their visit and for the valuable insights they shared. We look forward to continuing this exchange in the years ahead! 🙂

One outdated instrument document can quietly delay an entire commissioning schedule.

Here are 5 instrument and electrical documents EPC teams should keep 
synchronized at all times:

1️⃣ Instrument Index
The master list. If the index and the datasheets disagree, every document 
downstream inherits the error.

2️⃣ Instrument Datasheets
Specifications must match the process data and the vendor's final selection, 
not the first design revision.

3️⃣ Loop Diagrams
These are what the commissioning team actually uses on site. Outdated loops mean rework during loop checks.

4️⃣ Cable Schedule
Cable types, lengths, and routing change as the design matures. If the 
schedule is not updated, procurement and installation drift apart.

5️⃣ I/O List
It connects instrumentation, control system, and wiring. A mismatch here 
usually surfaces late, when it is most expensive to fix.

Most of these problems are not technical failures. They are document 
control failures.

posts.text:
Indonesia's coders multiplied by eight. Job ads for them fell by two-thirds.

I spent the last few weeks reading 284,000 archived job ads from Southeast Asian job sites, going back to 2019. I wanted to know one thing: are Indonesian companies still hiring the people who build software?

The short answer is fewer of them. In 2019–22, about 9.2 in every 100 Indonesian job ads were for software engineers. In 2024–26 it was 3.3. Over the same years the number of Indonesians pushing code to GitHub went from 104,000 to 804,000 a quarter.

Three things surprised me:

1. It happened on every site I could follow. On the professional board the software share went from 17.6% in 2019 to 9.9% in 2026. On the app-first board, from 15.6% in 2021 to 2.6% in 2025.
2. The space went to jobs you cannot do from a laptop. Logistics went from 4.8% to 8.4% of ads, operations and admin from 8.1% to 12.0%, finance and accounting from 8.1% to 11.4%.
3. AI barely shows up in the ads yet. In 2026, 2.3% of ads on the professional board mention generative AI.

I also wrote down bets for December 2027, but only for series where the method passed a backtest first (17 of 26 did). I will score them in public in January 2028.

The full story, with every chart and the method, is in the first comment.

🔊 WHAT IF THE NEXT GENERATION OF ACOUSTIC MATERIALS STARTED WITH A COCONUT HUSK? 🥥

When we think about acoustic panels, we often picture synthetic foam, mineral wool, fiberglass, or other conventional materials.
But what about natural fibers?

🌴 Coconut husk containscocofiber—a material traditionally associated with ropes, mats, brushes, and various industrial applications. Its potential may extend much further.

🔬 Natural fibers are an interesting area of acoustic material research because their fibrous structures can help dissipate sound energy under suitable material and design conditions.

This raises an interesting question:
COULD COCOFIBER BECOME A MATERIAL OPTION FOR ACOUSTIC-PANEL DEVELOPMENT?

For manufacturers and material developers exploring this possibility, several characteristics deserve attention:
🧵 1. FIBER STRUCTURE
Fiber length, distribution, thickness, and consistency can influence the structure and properties of the resulting acoustic material.
📐 2. DENSITY AND THICKNESS
These are important design variables that can influence the sound absorption characteristics of a fibrous panel.
🌬️ 3. POROSITY AND AIRFLOW RESISTANCE
The arrangement of fibers and the resulting pore structure influence how sound waves interact with and travel through the material.
🧱 4. MATERIAL COMPOSITION
Binders, backing materials, fiber treatment, and overall panel construction can influence the final acoustic and mechanical properties.
🔥 5. SAFETY AND DURABILITY
Fire performance, moisture resistance, dimensional stability, and long-term behavior must be evaluated for the intended application.

⚠️ ONE IMPORTANT DISTINCTION: SOUND ABSORPTION IS NOT THE SAME AS SOUNDPROOFING.
An acoustic panel may help reduce reflected sound and reverberation inside a room.
However, that does not automatically mean it can prevent sound from travelling between rooms.

The opportunity is not to claim that cocofiber can immediately replace conventional acoustic materials. It is to explore whether this agricultural fiber can be engineered into a material that meets specific acoustic, mechanical, safety, and commercial requirements.

📈 THIS IS WHERE MATERIAL INNOVATION BECOMES INTERESTING.
An agricultural by-product can become the starting point for research and development in an entirely different industrial sector.

💬 Could coconut fiber have a place in the future of acoustic materials?
We welcome perspectives from acoustic engineers, interior-material manufacturers, architects, and material developers.

As a chemical export professional at Sanyue, walking into the Canton Fair Complex for my very first CHINACOAT 2026 felt like stepping into the heartbeat of the global coatings industry.

From the first handshake to the last "let's keep in touch," I saw how trust is built in B2B trade: one honest conversation at a time. At Sanyue, we're already living this future. Our strategic partnerships span Vietnam, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, and beyond — a growing global service network built on the same principle: stay grounded in real-world application scenarios, and let customer pain points drive our R&D forward.

CHINACOAT 2026 may have closed its doors, but the conversations we started are just getting warmed up. If we met at our booth, or if you're exploring reliable partners in pigment coloring and silicone additive solutions — my inbox is open.

Why Civil Engineers Should Understand Spatial Planning — Not Just Construction.
One of the most valuable perspectives in civil engineering is understanding what happens before a project reaches the construction stage.
A development project may be technically feasible but still face significant challenges due to land-use regulations, infrastructure limitations, or spatial planning requirements.
Before starting construction, several important questions should be addressed:
1. Land Use Compatibility
Is the proposed development consistent with the applicable spatial planning framework?
2. Infrastructure Accessibility
Can existing roads, drainage networks, and utilities support the proposed development?
3. Site Constraints
Are there flood risks, environmental limitations, elevation differences, or other physical constraints?
4. Regulatory Considerations
What spatial planning and development requirements apply to the project?
5. Long-Term Development Impact
How will the project interact with surrounding infrastructure and future urban growth?
These considerations are particularly relevant in rapidly developing urban areas.
My professional background combines:
• 5+ years of experience in civil engineering and property development
• Exposure to development-related technical and project considerations
• Current professional experience within the spatial planning environment of Semarang City Government, Indonesia
This combination has helped me appreciate the relationship between engineering decisions, development feasibility, and regulatory considerations.
I believe civil engineers can contribute greater value when they understand the complete development lifecycle:
Planning → Feasibility → Engineering → Construction → Operation

posts.text:
🚨 AI won't replace recruiters.
But recruiters who use AI well will close hires 2x faster than those who don't.
Last month, my AI-assisted workflow helped me shortlist 6 AI engineers in Singapore in 4 days — for a role that had been open for 2 months.
Here's how I use AI + my ATS across the FULL hiring cycle 👇

1⃣ INTAKE ChatGPT/Claude turns a vague JD into a clear checklist: must-haves vs. nice-to-haves + smart questions for the hiring manager call.

2⃣ MARKET INTEL Perplexity Pro shows which companies are hiring a skill in SG/MY — with source links, so I verify everything myself.

3⃣ SOURCING AI drafts Boolean strings & similar titles (SRE, Platform Engineer, MLOps...). Then I hunt where candidates actually are: LinkedIn Recruiter, GitHub, JobStreet, Naukri, Indeed. → AI drafts. I decide.

4⃣ SCREENING — MY SKILL MATRIX 📊 A report card for every resume: ✅ proof shown • 🟡 needs checking • ❌ ask directly.

For an AI Engineer role: ✅ LLM fine-tuning — resume shows a project with real accuracy results → strong proof 🟡 RAG pipelines — mentioned, no outcomes → probe in screening ❌ MLOps — not shown → ask in the call

How the tools fit in, every day: 🤖 ChatGPT & Claude → build the checklist + draft screening questions 🤖 Gemini → explains any new tech in plain English in minutes 🧑‍💼 Me → I read every resume and make the final call. AI prepares. I decide.
I strip personal details first — fair hiring, every time.

5⃣ OUTREACH AI writes draft #1. I rewrite it around the candidate's real story. Copy-paste messages get ignored.

6⃣ OFFER, COMPLIANCE & JOINING Salary negotiation — where the human conversation matters most. For Singapore: EP rules, CPF, TAFEP fair-hiring checks, BGV. I verify every rule myself.

7⃣ ATS = SINGLE SOURCE OF TRUTH Workday • Ceipal • Zoho • Bullhorn — every stage tracked. No candidate falls through the cracks.
That's how I keep an ~80% offer-to-join ratio. 📈

⚠️ MY 3 NON-NEGOTIABLE RULES: 🔒 No confidential data in public AI tools ✅ Verify facts & regulations before sharing 🧠 AI never makes the hiring decision. People do.
Tools are the easy part. Trust, speed and market knowledge close the offer. 🤝

Global Talent Recruitment
Global Talent Recruitment connects skilled professionals with remote opportunities at companies around the world.
We are building a global candidate network for professionals seeking flexible, remote, and project-based work opportunities across multiple industries and functions.
Our focus includes:
• Software Engineering and Quality Assurance (QA)
 • Data Analysis and Data Operations
 • Customer Support and Business Operations
 • Finance and Accounting
 • Marketing and Project Management
 • AI Training, Evaluation, and Research Projects
 • Language, Voice, and Localization Projects
 • Administrative and Virtual Assistant Roles
We work with candidates from diverse professional backgrounds and help connect them with opportunities offered through our trusted hiring partners and employer networks.
How Our Process Works
Candidates express their interest in available opportunities.
We provide guidance and refer suitable candidates to trusted third-party hiring platforms.
Candidates may be required to complete assessments, including AI-powered or camera-based interviews, depending on employer requirements.
Employers and partner platforms review applications and make final hiring decisions.
Candidates are encouraged to apply to multiple suitable opportunities to increase their chances of finding a role that matches their skills and experience.
What Candidates Can Expect
• No recruitment fees for candidates.
 • Transparent application process.
 • Access to remote opportunities across different industries.
 • Opportunities ranging from entry-level roles to professional and specialized positions.
 • Flexible projects, contract work, and long-term opportunities depending on employer needs.
We may receive referral compensation from partner platforms when candidates successfully secure and begin qualifying opportunities. This does not affect the candidate's application process and never results in any fee charged to applicants.
Please note that Global Talent Recruitment functions as a talent referral and recruitment network. Hiring decisions, interviews, compensation, and final candidate selection are determined solely by employers and partner platforms.
Candidate Requirements
Successful candidates typically possess:
• Professional working English
 • Strong communication skills
 • Reliable internet access
 • A professional remote work environment
 • Willingness to complete required assessments and interviews
Our Mission
We believe talent has no borders. Our mission is to help qualified professionals access legitimate remote opportunities while helping employers discover capable talent from around the world.
Based in Jakarta, Indonesia. Working with candidates globally.
Follow our page for new remote job opportunities, hiring updates, and career resources.

A smelter does not run on ore alone.

It runs on ERP, sensors, a reporting line to head office abroad, and someone who knows what to do when the dashboard goes red at 2am.

Indonesia took in about IDR 270 trillion of foreign direct investment in Q3, up 27.5% year on year. Base metals led. GDP grew 5.47%, ahead of forecasts.

Everyone is calling it a factory story.

Concrete gets poured on schedule. Systems get bought on schedule. The people who keep them alive get found after the first incident.

Ask any plant manager what hurts more: a late machine or a missing engineer.

So who is planning that bench right now? Often nobody, because the budget line says plant, not platform.

Capital moves in a quarter.

Capability takes years.

posts.text:
If you employ people in Bangkok, Jakarta or Nairobi through a UK pension scheme, April 2027 is your problem too.

From 6 April 2027, unused defined contribution pots fall into the member's estate for inheritance tax.

Death-in-service lump sums from registered schemes stay outside.

Your overseas staff will not know the difference. Most of them think "the pension" and "the life cover" are the same thing.

Here's what changes for you as the employer.

Your scheme becomes part of the tax collection process. Executors can tell it to withhold up to half of a death benefit. Information requests come with 28-day deadlines. Payment notices with 35. A scheme that ignores a valid withholding notice can end up jointly liable for the tax.

Now picture that with a family in Chiang Mai or Mombasa, a Will written in another country, and a nomination form signed in 2014.

And don't assume this only touches British staff. Whether a South African engineer or a Filipino finance manager who never lived in the UK long-term is caught is exactly the cross-border question HMRC still hasn't answered.

What I'd be doing now if I ran HR or the scheme:

→ Pull a list of members living outside the UK
→ Get nomination forms refreshed, in writing, this quarter
→ Send a plain-English note separating death-in-service from the DC pot
→ Ask your administrator how they'll handle notices from overseas executors
→ Give staff access to proper advice, rather than giving it yourself

It's cheaper than the call you'll get from a widow's lawyer in 2028.

If your company has staff in Asia or Africa on a UK scheme, I'm happy to talk it through.

posts.text:
I spent last week walking through the facilities of X Origin in Shenzhen, asking one question.

What should a 12-year-old from Singapore, Jakarta or Kuala Lumpur actually learn about robots?

Robotics education for children in China has quietly changed.

It is no longer snapping plastic bricks together to static robot with limited movements.

Robotics and embodied-AI companies are now in the room.
They co-design curricula with education companies.
They set up labs inside schools.
They open their own sites so students can program real robotic arms and watch humanoid robots walk.

Not because the toys got better.
But because children are now learning on the same technology the industry is building.

I see the gap every time I bring overseas students into the Greater Bay Area.

Back home, many robotics classes are still at toy level.
Here, a student watches a robot in action in the morning.
In the afternoon, they write the code that tells it what to do.

Watching a robot and programming one are not the same.
A kit is not a curriculum. It is a toy.

So I am preparing courses for overseas students built around that exposure:

1. Hands-on sessions with real hardware, not only simulations
2. A path that starts with graphical programming for younger students and moves to Python for teenagers
3. Time with engineers, so robotics looks like a career and not just a hobby
4. Facility visits inside our GBA immersion programmes, so students see the whole chain from R&D to the production floor

If you are a parent in ASEAN, are you preparing your child for this, or just signing them up for another toy class?

Imho, young people in ASEAN should not only read about that change.

They should get their hands on it.

#Robotics #EmbodiedAI #STEMEducation #GreaterBayArea #China #ASEAN

$$5 Billion #REIT deal betweenBlackstone andAmazon Web Services (AWS) Datacenter & How Indonesian conglomerates like#Sinarmas, #Astra can replicate it?

On November 16, 2026, Blackstone Digital Infrastructure Trust#BXDC —a publicly traded#RealEstateInvestmentTrust managed by Blackstone—agreed to buy a majority stake in a portfolio of Amazon data centers.

Assets: 13 newly constructed powered shells equipped with power and cooling infrastructure, ready for servers) located in northern#Indiana &#Mississippi

Split: BXDC acquired 75% majority stake Amazon retains 25%

Capitalization rate annual yield 7%.

Capital Deployment: BXDC funding using proceeds from May 2026 #IPO

✅Triple-Net Leaseback: AWS will lease back 100% of the DC from the JV for an initial term of 12 years, options to extend upto 32 years. AWS continues to pay all property taxes, insurance, and maintenance costs while paying rent to the JV

✅Why AWS Sold: unlocks billions in cash to reinvest into high-margin tech, chips, and AI development. 

✅Why Blackstone Bought: predictable, inflation-protected cash flows, roughly $350 million in annual net operating income with zero #ConstructionRisk.

✅Long-Term Strategy?
Packaging these assets into a publicly traded REIT, Blackstone can continuously raise money from everyday retail and #institutionalinvestors to become the dominant landlord of the AI era.

✅What Indonesia Can Learn From This?

#CapitalRecycling via REITs (DIRE). Local telecommunications firms (likeTelkom Indonesia ) and developers carry heavy debt to build DC. Indonesia has its own REIT framework known as#DIRE #DanaInvestasiRealEstat. Local operators can use sale-leaseback models with DIRE structures to unlock cash from existing facilities and fund new builds

Indonesian #SovereignWealthFunds (such asDanantara Indonesia ) and private developers#Sinarmas #Astra can structure similar 75/25 joint ventures with global#infrastructurefunds to share risk and attract foreign direct investment

SinarMas is uniquely positioned to replicate Blackstone’s model because it already controls every piece of the value chain—land, power, fiber, telecoms, financial services, and an active data center platform#SMplus SM+

Step-by-step blueprint:

1.Land & Special Economic Zones. Through#SinarMasLand and PT Bumi Serpong Damai Tbk#BSD, the group owns vast land banks, including the D-Hub Special Economic Zone (SEZ) in BSD City, where PT Dian Swastatika Sentosa Tbk #DSSA recently secured 16.6 hectares specifically for data center expansion. Sinar Mas can build large-scale powered shells here with streamlined SEZ tax and permit incentives.

2 Energy & Connectivity: via DSSA and massive fiber-optic and telecom networks viaPT XLSMART Telecom Sejahtera Tbk , Bundling land, dedicated green power, and dark fiber allows Sinar Mas to deliver turnkey powered shells faster than standalone developers

Step 3-6 are in comment section.

How can we help customers launch refueling stations faster in emerging markets? 🌍
This was a key focus of my presentation at IG Indonesia 2026 in Jakarta, where I represented BLUESKY and shared our modular CNG, LNG and L-CNG solutions, alongside integrated hydrogen equipment.
Drawing on our project experience in Nigeria and Jamaica, I discussed how skid-mounted and containerized equipment can help customers move from project planning to market entry.
For developers in Nigeria and other emerging markets, the right configuration can make a practical difference:
🔹 Faster deployment
Factory assembly allows much of the internal piping, wiring and equipment integration to be completed before shipment, while the local team prepares the site.
🔹 Less on-site installation work
Clearly defined equipment packages and connections can simplify installation and help control local labor costs.
🔹 Solutions matched to the available gas supply
Pipeline-fed CNG stations, trailer-supplied daughter stations and L-CNG stations offer different routes to serving local demand.
🔹 Room to grow
A suitable modular design can support phased investment and future expansion as vehicle numbers and fuel demand increase.
Our approach starts with your gas source, target customers, daily demand and site conditions. From there, we develop a customized equipment configuration and coordinate installation guidance, commissioning and operator training.
During the trip, I also visited local hydrogen facilities at PLN Indonesia Power’s Hydrogen Center, gaining a closer view of Indonesia’s hydrogen infrastructure.
Thank you to the organizers, our hosts and everyone who visited our booth.
Planning a refueling business in Nigeria or another emerging market? Let’s discuss how BLUESKY can help you reduce on-site work, accelerate deployment and start serving customers sooner.

The goal of this challenge was to fill the gap. I simply wanted to get more comfortable with Xcode, and somewhere along the way, it became an iPhone with Watch app companion on the App Store.

It was individual challenge at Apple Developer Academy @ UC, Jakarta, so everything from design to development was on me. As a designer, the development part was where I wanted to push myself the most.

The app is called MyBudgetGweh, a simple expense tracker. You can log your income and spending in a few taps, check where your money went each month, and even add entries straight from your Apple Watch using the Digital Crown, plus a voice note if you’re too lazy to type. Everything stays on your device, so no sign-up or so on.

Honestly, most of my time went into figuring things out: how to structure the code, how to get the iPhone and Apple Watch apps talking to each other, and a lot of trial and error in between. On top of that, I implemented some of Apple’s Accessibility Nutrition Labels, from Larger Text and Dark Interface to Sufficient Contrast.

Seeing something I designed actually running on my wrist is still a pretty fun feeling and I’m excited to keep improving it. Feel free to try it out, link’s in the comments!

posts.text:
In 2010 a small Jakarta team gave local developers something to be proud of. On 25 May 2010, Yahoo announced it had acquired Koprol, an Indonesian location-based social network. Koprol launched in February 2009 and worked straight from an ordinary phone browser, no GPS and no special app needed. You checked in to a place and saw who else was there.

Why it still matters to me: Koprol won because it was built for the phones Indonesians actually carried back then, not the phones we wished they had. But the story is also a warning. In mid 2012 Yahoo decided to shut the service down, and a month later it handed the trademark and domain rights back to the founders.

The lesson for me: learn your users' real devices and habits, and build from there. And don't assume that being bought by a big player means your product is safe forever. If you're building an app today, have you tried it on your users' most basic phone?

Source: https://lnkd.in/gCHSwuBg
https://lnkd.in/gRUF7RtB

Day 63 | 100+ Days Full Stack Developer Challenge 🚀

Moving one step deeper into Advanced Java — today, I completed HTTP Request & Response Handling using Jakarta Servlets.
After learning Servlet fundamentals and lifecycle management, I focused on understanding how browsers communicate with Java applications and how servlets inspect incoming requests and construct appropriate HTTP responses.
The goal was to move beyond theory and implement these concepts through practical programs.

🔹 What I Implemented
I successfully completed 7 practical Servlet programs:
HTTP Request Inspector – Explored request methods, URI, URL, query strings and server information.
HTTP Response Builder – Configured response status, custom headers, content types and character encoding.
HTTP Header Inspector – Examined User-Agent, Accept, Accept-Language, Host, Referer and header enumeration.
HTTP Status Code Handler – Worked with 200, 201, 400, 401, 403, 404 and 500 status codes.
Content Type Handler – Generated HTML, JSON and plain-text responses.
Character Encoding Handler – Implemented UTF-8 encoding and multilingual character rendering.
Request Parameter Validator – Handled missing parameters, empty values and multiple parameter values.

🔹 Key Technical Understanding
Two important Servlet components played a central role:
HttpServletRequest – Provides access to incoming request information, headers, parameters and client details.
HttpServletResponse – Helps configure the outgoing response, including status codes, headers, content type and encoding.
Understanding how these two components work together is essential for building Java-based web applications.

🔹 Technology Stack
Java 21 | Jakarta Servlet | Apache Tomcat 10.1 | Eclipse IDE | HTML5 | CSS3 | HTTP
📌 Day 63 — Successfully Completed
Seven practical programs, deeper HTTP understanding, and more hands-on experience with server-side Java development.
The journey continues as I strengthen my Advanced Java fundamentals and progress towards Java Full Stack development.
One more day of learning. One more step towards becoming a better engineer.
